one_line: Alex Shaw (Terminal-Bench, Harbor) argues agents behave like ML models, so teams should build environments (instruction, sandbox, verifier) and run parallel rollouts for evals, training data, RL and agentic map-reduce.
summary: Alex Shaw of the Laude Institute opens by contrasting 2018 software engineering, where code behavior was predictable before running it, with 2026 agent development, where a model call makes the program's output probabilistic. He quotes Francois Chollet's view that generated code is a black-box artifact to be managed by empirical evaluation, and extends it to agent performance in general. He maps machine-learning concepts onto agent development: training data and evals become environments, weights become skills, prompts, tools and the model, and gradient steps become pull requests. An environment has three parts: an instruction, a sandbox and a verifier, specified as a standard file directory. Harbor is presented as the open-source format and framework that runs these rollouts in parallel with any agent, model and sandbox, with a registry of several hundred eval sets. The talk lists four eval types teams build (internal coding, agent usability of their product, agent-powered features, and internal process automation) and several non-eval uses such as agentic map-reduce over session logs. It closes with downstream uses (SFT, RL, text-based hill-climbing on trajectories) and a list of benchmarks built on Harbor.

key_ideas.idea: Agent performance should be treated as a black-box ML artifact measured empirically
key_ideas.detail: Speaker contrasts 2018 code, where a regex's output is certain, with a 2026 model-call program whose output is probabilistic. He extends Chollet's point about generated code to agent behavior in general.

key_ideas.idea: Agent development maps onto ML with new names
key_ideas.detail: Training data and evals become environments; weights become skills, prompts, tools and the model choice; the loss becomes environment rewards; the optimizer becomes context-based optimization (a text optimizer, captioned as 'JEPA'); a gradient step becomes a pull request; overfitting becomes reward hacking. Tooling for the left column exists, the right column is early.

key_ideas.idea: An environment is instruction + sandbox + verifier, written as a directory
key_ideas.detail: The instruction tells the agent the task, the sandbox is a virtual computer where it acts, and the verifier (tests, rubric or an agent) decides whether it succeeded. Harbor specifies this as a file directory layout that the speaker says has become a fairly standard format, so environments can move between teams.

key_ideas.idea: A rollout is a fixed loop whose trajectory matters as much as the final reward
key_ideas.detail: Start sandbox, run agent until a stop condition, keep the trajectory, pass the sandbox to the verifier, stop the sandbox, record reward(s), then aggregate across a dataset. Harbor adds multi-step runs, separate verifier sandboxes, artifact collection and simulated users on top of this base.

key_ideas.idea: Build the eval first, then optimize against it, and welcome all models
key_ideas.detail: He quotes Satya Nadella: start with the eval that matters and your ability to grade the outcome, then consider any model. Owning the grader lets a team pick the cost-performance point on the Pareto frontier rather than trust a vendor or public benchmark.

key_ideas.idea: Every company that uses computers should build agent evals
key_ideas.detail: He argues nearly all companies qualify, because any computer-based process is a candidate for automation. He lists four eval types that Harbor users build: how well agents build your product (internal codebase benchmarks, e.g. a Ramp SWE-bench-style set), how well agents use your product (headless mode), how well agents power product features, and how well agents automate internal processes.

key_ideas.idea: Harbor also serves as a fan-out engine for non-eval jobs
key_ideas.detail: Agentic map-reduce runs many agents in parallel sandboxes, then aggregates results. The demo maps over 32 Codex sessions with a cheap, fast model (Cursor CLI) and reduces them with a stronger model to summarize recurring mistakes into a feedback file. He notes this use case emerged from users rather than being planned.

key_ideas.idea: Trajectories and rewards feed training and optimization downstream
key_ideas.detail: People use rollouts for SFT, for RL with rewards (Tinker has an integration), and for evolutionary or hill-climbing loops that use text feedback from trajectories and evals to improve a harness or skill. He also mentions a multi-billion-dollar market in which experts write tasks and sell them to labs.

techniques.name: Environment as a three-part directory (instruction, sandbox, verifier)
techniques.how: Specify each task as a directory with the instruction for the agent, the sandboxed starting state, and a verifier made of programmatic tests, rubrics, or an agent. Keep it in a shared layout so tasks can be swapped between tools.
techniques.when: Use when you want evals or training data that are portable across agents, models and sandbox providers.

techniques.name: Separate rollout, trajectory capture and verification
techniques.how: Run the agent in a fresh sandbox until a stop condition, store the full trajectory, then hand the sandbox to a verifier that produces a reward. Aggregate rewards across the dataset to get the eval score.
techniques.when: Use when you need to diagnose failures later from the trajectory, not just the pass/fail score, or when you may reuse trajectories for SFT or RL.

techniques.name: Parallel rollouts with a fire-and-forget launch
techniques.how: Launch many rollouts at once (the demo uses 64 parallel workers) and let a hosted runner execute them, so results arrive later instead of blocking the terminal.
techniques.when: Use when a rollout takes a long time and the loop needs to run at high throughput overnight.

techniques.name: Agentic map-reduce over agent logs
techniques.how: Map: a cheap, fast model reviews each session and writes a structured record (mistake, reason, correction). Reduce: a stronger model reads the records and summarizes recurring failure categories into a feedback file. Run each map step in its own sandbox.
techniques.when: Use when you need to mine many agent sessions for patterns and can afford to spend more compute on the summary step.

techniques.name: Own the eval before choosing a model
techniques.how: Build a grader for the outcome that matters to your business, such as an internal codebase benchmark. Then compare models and coding agents against it instead of trusting public leaderboards.
techniques.when: Use when picking a coding agent or model for your own product, or when token spend needs to be justified.

techniques.name: Design for agent users of your product
techniques.how: Measure how well agents complete tasks through your product's headless interface, then change the product to fix the failures the eval reveals.
techniques.when: Use when your product has an API or CLI that agents will call, and you want more agent usage.

tools: A frontier model transcribed as 'Fable 5' (reduce step in demo; name may be a caption error)

numbers.claim: Harbor registry holds roughly 300 to 400 eval sets (speaker's approximate count)
Two or three new benchmarks launched the same day run on Harbor
Demo eval runs 64 rollouts in parallel on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with Codex and GPT-5.5; the launch feature can run around 10,000 rollouts unattended on Harbor servers
Agent builder and user population is claimed to be probably an order of magnitude larger than the number who ever did machine learning (speaker's estimate)
A market for expert-written tasks sold to model labs is described as multi-billion dollars (speaker's estimate)
Agentic map-reduce demo capped at 32 Codex session logs

hot_takes: Agent development is closer to machine learning than to traditional software engineering, so agent behavior should be managed as a black box with empirical evals.
Nearly every company that uses computers should be building agent evals now, since any computer-based process is a candidate for automation.
Once you own a grader for your outcome, you no longer need to trust a model vendor's or a public benchmark's claims.

relevance.why: Harbor's environment format (instruction, sandbox, verifier) and rollout loop are a reusable reference for evaluating sandboxed code-execution in Crucible, but the talk does not cover AgentOS's proxy or KV-cache work.
relevance.action: Read the Harbor docs on the environment directory layout and compare it with what Crucible would need to define an eval task.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps the Claude Code CLI for long runs, and this talk gives a concrete way to evaluate such runs as sandboxed rollouts with stored trajectories and verifiers, which could check checkpoint/resume and plan quality.
relevance.action: Write one ProsHarness task (instruction, sandbox, verifier) for a checkpoint/resume run and try a parallel rollout of it on Harbor to see if the harness is measurably better.
